questions.explanation: The relevant evidence is the thesis itself, stated carefully. The harm principle permits coercion only to prevent harm to others. This is the position defended by John Stuart Mill. The claim that the harm principle permits coercion to prevent any offense is a common mistake about the view, often described as "conflates harm with offense". A fair assessment also has to reckon with this worry: harm is hard to define. Noting what the position does and does not claim resolves the matter.
questions.hint: Ask what critics of the harm principle most often find problematic.
